standard.title: Sustaining democracy and cohesion
standard.description: the challenges to and ways of sustaining a resilient democracy and a cohesive society in Australia and/or in our region or globally
standard.prior_knowledge: Students know how individuals and groups participate in and contribute to civic life in Australia and to global citizenship (AC9HC9K05). They understand the influence of media, including social media, in shaping identity and attitudes to diversity (AC9HC9K06).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the challenges to and ways of sustaining a resilient democracy and a cohesive society, examining threats and responses in the Australian and/or global context.

nodes.label: Characteristics of a resilient democracy and cohesive society
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the key characteristics of cohesive, democratic societies and explain why an active and informed citizenry is important for sustaining them.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least three key characteristics of cohesive, democratic societies and explain why each matters.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the key characteristics of cohesive, democratic societies — cooperation, inclusion, respect, peaceful resolution of conflicts, and an active and informed citizenry — and examine how these characteristics reinforce each other.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians have articulated the conditions needed for a cohesive and democratic Australia (e.g. through the Uluru Statement from the Heart) and compare with mainstream democratic theory
Explore what 'active citizenship' requires in practice and examine examples of citizens who have strengthened democratic resilience
Examine international research on what makes democracies resilient over time and evaluate how Australia compares
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't have a clear model of what a resilient democracy looks like cannot identify what constitutes a threat to it — the threat analysis in the next node requires a baseline understanding of what is being threatened.

response_modes.reason: Students often have intuitive but vague notions of democracy. Invest in building a precise, multi-dimensional model before examining threats — the quality of threat analysis depends on how clearly the baseline is defined.

The Uluru Statement direction connects the characteristics of a cohesive democracy to an active civic document produced by First Nations Australians — this is a richer starting point than abstract theory alone.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Uluru Statement direction is substantively rich — it gives students a concrete and contested Australian document to examine, connecting democratic theory to live civic debate rather than treating it as settled.
success_criteria: Identifies at least three characteristics of cohesive, democratic societies
Explains why an active and informed citizenry is important for sustaining democracy
Uses accurate civics terminology (e.g. civic participation, social cohesion)

nodes.label: Threats to democratic resilience
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and discuss a range of threats to Australian democracy and democratic societies more broadly, including vested interests, corruption, and the impact of social media on civic debate.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two threats to democratic resilience and explain how each undermines key democratic characteristics.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and discuss a range of threats to Australian democracy and other democracies — vested interests, organised crime, corruption and lawlessness, the impact of social media on civic debate quality, extreme polarisation, breakdown of social consensus, and the rise of non-democratic extremist groups — with specific examples.
wider: Investigate how social media disinformation campaigns have affected civic debate quality in Australia and at least one other democracy, comparing the scale and nature of impact
Examine the rise of extremism in a specific democratic context and analyse what conditions allowed non-democratic forces to gain influence
Locate and evaluate data on public trust in democratic institutions in Australia over time and assess what the trends suggest about threats to resilience

response_modes.reason: The range of threat types is wide and students benefit from encountering examples across multiple categories (social media, corruption, extremism) rather than treating one type as the only threat.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Social media disinformation and the rise of extremism are live, contested phenomena — examining them comparatively (Australia plus another democracy) gives students analytical distance and richer evidence than a single-country focus.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two distinct types of threat to democratic resilience
Explains how each threat undermines at least one characteristic of a cohesive, democratic society
Uses specific examples or evidence to support the analysis

nodes.label: Ways of sustaining democracy and social cohesion
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss ways of sustaining democratic resilience and social cohesion, including through public debate, civic participation, and engagement with controversial issues.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two ways individuals, groups or institutions can sustain democratic resilience or social cohesion, using a specific example for at least one.
nodes.typical_width: Examine how Western democratic heritage and values — including freedom of speech — support participation in public debate about controversial issues, and discuss how citizens and institutions can sustain democratic resilience and social cohesion through specific practices and choices.
wider: Examine a specific controversial public debate (e.g. the date of Australia Day, the Uluru Statement, reconciliation and treaty) and evaluate how the democratic system has handled it — what worked, what failed
Investigate how a non-government organisation or civic movement has worked to sustain social cohesion in Australia, and assess its effectiveness
Explore how countries in the region have responded to threats to democratic resilience and compare their approaches with Australia's

response_modes.reason: The Australia Day date / Uluru Statement / treaty directions are examples of live, contested public debates where students can examine democratic processes in action — these give the abstract concept of 'sustaining democracy' concrete form.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The live Australian debates (Australia Day, Uluru Statement, treaty) are not just additional examples — they are sites where democratic resilience is actively being tested. Engaging with them gives students authentic civic material rather than textbook cases.
success_criteria: Describes at least two ways of sustaining democratic resilience or social cohesion
Explains how freedom of speech supports participation in public debate
Uses a specific example of a controversial public debate to illustrate the point

nodes.label: Evaluating Australia's democratic resilience
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate Australia's democratic resilience, considering both threats and responses, and connect this to the responsibilities of active citizenship.
nodes.minimum_width: Offer a supported judgement about Australia's democratic resilience, identifying both a significant threat and an effective response.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate Australia's democratic resilience by weighing significant threats against existing responses and mechanisms, and connect this evaluation to what active, informed citizenship requires in the current civic environment.
wider: Evaluate the adequacy of Australia's democratic institutions in addressing reconciliation, truth-telling and First Nations sovereignty, and assess what a more resilient, cohesive democracy would require
Compare Australia's democratic resilience with that of another democracy in the region, drawing evidence-based conclusions
Argue a position on a specific controversial issue (e.g. call for a treaty, Uluru Statement) as an exercise in democratic participation, using evidence and acknowledging opposing views

response_modes.reason: Integration node — characteristics of democracy, threat analysis, and responses come together in an evaluative argument about Australia's current situation. Teaching investment is in supporting students to move from description to supported evaluation.

success_criteria: Makes a supported evaluative claim about Australia's democratic resilience
Identifies at least one significant threat and at least one effective response
Connects the evaluation to the responsibilities of active citizenship
